title: Insider and related-company leases: when the building last changed hands
question: For City-funded nonprofits that reported a lease with an insider or a related company, when did the building at the address on the return last change hands, relative to the years the City has been paying the organization?
finding: The tax returns give no address for the leased premises, so the address on the return stands in for it: 27 San Francisco buildings for 25 organizations, 7 of them for leases with an insider. 2 of those buildings show a sale date in the years the City was paying the organization (0 of them insider leases): Compass Family Services at 37 Grove Street (sale dated 10 September 2018, value set $9,500,000; reported lease with COMPASS QALICB); Hamilton Families at 2567 Mission St (sale dated 7 February 2023, value set $8,262,000; reported lease with HAMILTON FAMILIES QALICB). Both are related-organization leases, the usual form when a nonprofit buys its own building through a company it controls. The roll names no owners, so none of this shows that an insider or a related company was the buyer.
how: The insider and related-organization leases in the property screens (IRS Form 990, Schedules L and R), with the address the download step attached to each: the organization’s own address on its latest return or, for a related organization, that organization’s address. Each address was matched to a parcel and its roll history read from 2007 to 2025. City payments are the fiscal years with payments in the organization’s profile on this site (2019 on). A sale counts as “during” if its year falls from the year before the first payment on file to the last. Parcels the roll classes as single-family homes are left out, and insiders are described by the relationship the return reports, not by name.
limits: This is the weakest screen here and is kept so the gap is visible. The return does not say where the leased space is; an organization’s office is often not the space it rents from its insider. The roll names no owners, so a sale date at the address says nothing about who bought. A nonprofit holding its buildings through a related company is routine, and a board member renting space to a charity at or below market does it a favour. The roll records no price. The value that appears after a sale date is an indicator of the price, because California law re-sets assessed value to the price paid when a property changes hands; exemptions, a transfer of part of a property, transfers the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break that link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder would settle what was paid; neither is open data. The lease itself, and the deed for the address in it, would show who owns what.
